claim: Influenza virus genome sequencing is becoming cheaper, faster, and more readily available.
source: As influenza virus genome sequencing becomes cheaper, faster, and more readily available, the ability to predict pandemic potential from sequence data could transform pandemic influenza risk assessment capabilities.
evidence: This is stated as a premise in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations.

claim: The relationships between virus genotype and phenotype are complex.
source: However, the complexities of the relationships between virus genotype and phenotype make such predictions extremely difficult.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Direct experimental assessment of human-to-human transmission of potential pandemic viruses is not feasible.
source: For obvious reasons, direct experimental assessment of human-to-human transmission of potential pandemic viruses is not feasible.
evidence: This is stated as self-evident knowledge based on ethical considerations.

claim: Influenza viruses that have caused pandemics in humans transmit efficiently in ferret models.
source: However, influenza viruses that have caused pandemics in humans have been shown to transmit efficiently in animal models (most commonly ferrets) (Chou et al., 2011, Yen et al., 2011), thus animal models are thought to be useful for examining the genetic changes in viruses that facilitate human-to-human transmission.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou et al., 2011 and Yen et al., 2011.

claim: Animal models are useful for examining genetic changes in viruses that facilitate human-to-human transmission.
source: However, influenza viruses that have caused pandemics in humans have been shown to transmit efficiently in animal models (most commonly ferrets) (Chou et al., 2011, Yen et al., 2011), thus animal models are thought to be useful for examining the genetic changes in viruses that facilitate human-to-human transmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that pandemic viruses transmit in animal models.

claim: Genetic changes in the neuraminidase (NA) and matrix (M) gene segments acquired by the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus lineage increased transmissibility in animal models.
source: For example, several studies have shown that genetic changes in the neuraminidase (NA) and matrix (M) gene segments acquired by the virus lineage responsible for the 2009 H1N1 pandemic increased transmissibility in animal models (Chou et al., 2011, Lakdawala et al., 2011, Yen et al., 2011), suggesting that these changes may have played a role in enhancing the virus's transmissibility in humans and hence paved the way for pandemic emergence.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Chou et al., 2011, Lakdawala et al., 2011, Yen et al., 2011).

claim: Genetic changes in NA and M gene segments may have enhanced the 2009 H1N1 virus's transmissibility in humans and facilitated pandemic emergence.
source: For example, several studies have shown that genetic changes in the neuraminidase (NA) and matrix (M) gene segments acquired by the virus lineage responsible for the 2009 H1N1 pandemic increased transmissibility in animal models (Chou et al., 2011, Lakdawala et al., 2011, Yen et al., 2011), suggesting that these changes may have played a role in enhancing the virus's transmissibility in humans and hence paved the way for pandemic emergence.
evidence: This is presented as a speculation based on animal model data.

claim: Animal experiments can provide quantitative measures of virus traits that can be integrated into quantitative risk assessment measures such as IRAT.
source: When animal experiments provide quantitative measures of virus traits, these can be integrated into quantitative measures of risk assessment such as the IRAT (Trock et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trock et al., 2012.

claim: Gain-of-function studies have attempted to prospectively identify new mutations in avian H5N1 viruses that enhance airborne transmission between ferrets.
source: Recently, several high-profile and controversial gain-of-function (GoF) studies have attempted to go beyond the characterization of existing viruses to prospectively identify new mutations in avian H5N1 viruses that enhance the ability of these viruses to transmit between ferrets by the airborne route (Chen et al., 2012, Herfst et al., 2012, Imai et al., 2012, Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple GoF studies.

claim: There are more than 10^18 different possible five-mutation variants of any given hemagglutinin (HA).
source: Because of the vast size of genetic space, such studies cannot possibly delineate all genetic variants of a virus that might be transmissible—after all, there are more than 1018 different possible five-mutation variants of any given hemagglutinin (HA), which is more than what can reasonably be assayed experimentally and the vast majority will not facilitate transmissibility.
evidence: This is a calculation based on combinatorial mathematics.

claim: The vast majority of five-mutation variants of HA will not facilitate transmissibility.
source: Because of the vast size of genetic space, such studies cannot possibly delineate all genetic variants of a virus that might be transmissible—after all, there are more than 1018 different possible five-mutation variants of any given hemagglutinin (HA), which is more than what can reasonably be assayed experimentally and the vast majority will not facilitate transmissibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding that most random mutations are not beneficial.

claim: Switching receptor binding from avian-like α2,3 sialic acid to human-like α2,6 sialic acid linkages is a transmissibility trait identified by GoF studies.
source: Transmissibility traits identified by GoF studies to date include some that were already known (such as switching receptor binding from avian-like α2,3 sialic acid to human-like α2,6 sialic acid linkages (Yamada et al., 2006) and lowering the optimal temperature for viral polymerase activity (Massin et al., 2001)), as well as some that are new, such as increasing HA stability and reducing glycosylation on HA's globular head (Herfst et al., 2012, Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2006.

claim: Lowering the optimal temperature for viral polymerase activity is a transmissibility trait identified by GoF studies.
source: Transmissibility traits identified by GoF studies to date include some that were already known (such as switching receptor binding from avian-like α2,3 sialic acid to human-like α2,6 sialic acid linkages (Yamada et al., 2006) and lowering the optimal temperature for viral polymerase activity (Massin et al., 2001)), as well as some that are new, such as increasing HA stability and reducing glycosylation on HA's globular head (Herfst et al., 2012, Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Massin et al., 2001.

claim: Increasing HA stability is a new transmissibility trait identified by GoF studies.
source: Transmissibility traits identified by GoF studies to date include some that were already known (such as switching receptor binding from avian-like α2,3 sialic acid to human-like α2,6 sialic acid linkages (Yamada et al., 2006) and lowering the optimal temperature for viral polymerase activity (Massin et al., 2001)), as well as some that are new, such as increasing HA stability and reducing glycosylation on HA's globular head (Herfst et al., 2012, Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herfst et al., 2012 and Imai et al., 2012.

claim: Reducing glycosylation on HA's globular head is a new transmissibility trait identified by GoF studies.
source: Transmissibility traits identified by GoF studies to date include some that were already known (such as switching receptor binding from avian-like α2,3 sialic acid to human-like α2,6 sialic acid linkages (Yamada et al., 2006) and lowering the optimal temperature for viral polymerase activity (Massin et al., 2001)), as well as some that are new, such as increasing HA stability and reducing glycosylation on HA's globular head (Herfst et al., 2012, Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herfst et al., 2012 and Imai et al., 2012.

claim: It is unclear whether the transmissibility traits identified in GoF studies are necessary or sufficient for transmissibility among humans or other mammalian animal models.
source: Whether these traits are either necessary or sufficient for transmissibility among humans or even other mammalian animal models remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an explicit limitation of current knowledge.

claim: An avian H5N1 virus with internal genes reassorted from a 2009 pandemic virus became transmissible in guinea pigs despite retaining preference for α2,3 sialic acid binding.
source: For example, a recent study of an avian H5N1 virus found that by reassorting its internal genes with those of a 2009 pandemic virus, the virus could be rendered transmissible in guinea pigs (which have both α2,6 and α2,3 sialic acid in the upper respiratory tract) despite retaining a preference for binding α2,3 sialic acid.
evidence: This is described as a finding from a recent study, with citation to follow.

claim: Guinea pigs have both α2,6 and α2,3 sialic acid in the upper respiratory tract.
source: For example, a recent study of an avian H5N1 virus found that by reassorting its internal genes with those of a 2009 pandemic virus, the virus could be rendered transmissible in guinea pigs (which have both α2,6 and α2,3 sialic acid in the upper respiratory tract) despite retaining a preference for binding α2,3 sialic acid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about guinea pig biology.

claim: When mutations from ferret GoF experiments were used to switch H5N1 receptor specificity to α2,6 sialic acid in a reassortant virus, transmissibility was lost.
source: However, when mutations identified in earlier ferret GoF experiments were used to switch the receptor specificity to α2,6 sialic acid, transmissibility was lost (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The NA mutation H275Y consistently confers oseltamivir resistance on N1 neuraminidases.
source: Some mutations have been shown to be strong markers for phenotype for well-defined collections of viruses—for instance, the NA mutation H275Y consistently confers oseltamivir resistance on N1 neuraminidases (although the impact of the mutation on surface expression of NA, and thus virus fitness, varies dramatically) (Baz et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baz et al., 2010 and Bloom et al., 2010.

claim: The impact of the H275Y mutation on surface expression of NA and virus fitness varies dramatically.
source: Some mutations have been shown to be strong markers for phenotype for well-defined collections of viruses—for instance, the NA mutation H275Y consistently confers oseltamivir resistance on N1 neuraminidases (although the impact of the mutation on surface expression of NA, and thus virus fitness, varies dramatically) (Baz et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baz et al., 2010 and Bloom et al., 2010.

claim: The PB2 E627K substitution adapts the viral polymerase to mammalian cells in some viruses but not others.
source: Similarly, the PB2 E627K substitution adapts the viral polymerase to mammalian cells in some viruses (Long et al., 2013) but not others (Herfst et al., 2010), while other viruses have adapted to mammals via different substitutions in PB2 (Jagger et al., 2010, Mehle and Doudna, 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Long et al., 2013 and Herfst et al., 2010.

claim: Some viruses have adapted to mammals via different substitutions in PB2 other than E627K.
source: Similarly, the PB2 E627K substitution adapts the viral polymerase to mammalian cells in some viruses (Long et al., 2013) but not others (Herfst et al., 2010), while other viruses have adapted to mammals via different substitutions in PB2 (Jagger et al., 2010, Mehle and Doudna, 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jagger et al., 2010, Mehle and Doudna, 2009, and Zhu et al., 2010.

claim: The effects of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte escape mutations on nucleoprotein (NP) function depend on the stability of the parent protein.
source: In many cases, the effect of mutations can be highly sensitive to genetic context—for instance, the effects of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte escape mutations on nucleoprotein (NP) function depend on the stability of the parent protein, which can be affected by at least dozens of other mutations (Gong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gong et al., 2013.

claim: The stability of the parent NP protein can be affected by at least dozens of other mutations.
source: In many cases, the effect of mutations can be highly sensitive to genetic context—for instance, the effects of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte escape mutations on nucleoprotein (NP) function depend on the stability of the parent protein, which can be affected by at least dozens of other mutations (Gong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gong et al., 2013.

claim: Context dependence has been shown for receptor binding specificity substitutions in H5N1 viruses.
source: Similar patterns of context dependence have recently been shown for receptor binding specificity substitutions in H5N1 viruses (Tharakaraman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tharakaraman et al., 2013.

claim: Computational methods have higher throughput, shorter turnaround times, are cheaper, and are safer than experimental work with whole virulent viruses.
source: Computational methods present an attractive adjunct to experimental studies because they have higher throughput, have shorter turnaround times, are cheaper, and are safer than experimental work with whole virulent viruses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the advantages of computational methods.

claim: The main drawback of computational methods is the largely unknown accuracy of their predictions.
source: The main drawback of computational methods is the largely unknown accuracy of their predictions—a drawback that is exacerbated by the lack of an established framework for validating the accuracy of the numerous computational prediction methods that populate the literature.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of computational methods.

claim: There is a lack of an established framework for validating the accuracy of computational prediction methods.
source: The main drawback of computational methods is the largely unknown accuracy of their predictions—a drawback that is exacerbated by the lack of an established framework for validating the accuracy of the numerous computational prediction methods that populate the literature.
evidence: This is stated as a known gap in the field.

claim: Receptor-binding preference, antiviral susceptibility, antigenicity of HA and NA, and possibly T-cell epitopes are the elements of influenza pandemic risk assessment most amenable to computational prediction.
source: The elements of influenza pandemic risk assessment that are most amenable to computational prediction are those that correspond to well-defined, quantifiable molecular-scale traits such as receptor-binding preference, antiviral susceptibility, antigenicity of HA and NA, and possibly T-cell epitopes.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of which traits are suitable for computational prediction.

claim: Higher-level phenotypes such as transmissibility are not yet sufficiently well understood to be reasonable targets for computational predictions.
source: Higher-level phenotypes such as transmissibility, that integrate phenomena at a range of scales, are not yet sufficiently well understood to be reasonable targets for computational predictions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current understanding.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations that combine high- and low-fidelity models show promise for genotype-to-phenotype prediction.
source: A variety of computational methods shows promise for genotype-to-phenotype prediction including molecular dynamics simulations that combine high- and low-fidelity models (Amaro et al., 2009) and statistical learning approaches that use protein structure, dynamics, and sequence data to predict the phenotypic consequences of mutation (Kasson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amaro et al., 2009.

claim: Statistical learning approaches that use protein structure, dynamics, and sequence data show promise for predicting the phenotypic consequences of mutation.
source: A variety of computational methods shows promise for genotype-to-phenotype prediction including molecular dynamics simulations that combine high- and low-fidelity models (Amaro et al., 2009) and statistical learning approaches that use protein structure, dynamics, and sequence data to predict the phenotypic consequences of mutation (Kasson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kasson et al., 2009.

claim: Better prospective validation of computational tools against experimental data is essential before these tools can be reliably used for informing public health decisions or policymaking.
source: However, better prospective validation of these tools against experimental data, particularly for exploring context dependency of genetic changes, is essential before these tools can be reliably used for informing public health decisions or policymaking (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for future use of computational tools.

claim: CASP-like exercises could spur cooperation between experimental and computational scientists to produce consistent testing and validation data.
source: One possible mechanism to spur cooperation would be a series of regular community assessment exercises similar to Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP) (Moult et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the CASP model, with citation to Moult et al., 2011.

claim: Thermophoretic or interferometric measurements of HA binding affinities to α2,3- and α2,6-sialoglycans are ideal experimental data sets for CASP-like exercises.
source: Ideal experimental data sets for CASP-like exercises include thermophoretic or interferometric measurements of HA binding affinities to α2,3- and α2,6-sialoglycans (Xiong et al., 2013) and multi-method characterizations of viral pH activation shifts for sets of point mutants in HA (Galloway et al., 2013, Thoennes et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2013.

claim: Multi-method characterizations of viral pH activation shifts for sets of point mutants in HA are ideal experimental data sets for CASP-like exercises.
source: Ideal experimental data sets for CASP-like exercises include thermophoretic or interferometric measurements of HA binding affinities to α2,3- and α2,6-sialoglycans (Xiong et al., 2013) and multi-method characterizations of viral pH activation shifts for sets of point mutants in HA (Galloway et al., 2013, Thoennes et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galloway et al., 2013 and Thoennes et al., 2008.

claim: Reliable computational prediction of biochemical traits from genetic data would be a major accomplishment.
source: Reliable computational prediction of biochemical traits from genetic data would be a major accomplishment.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the significance of achieving this goal.

claim: Further major developments, particularly computational prediction of total virus fitness in new hosts, would be required for realizing the utility of computational tools in policymaking.
source: However, it should be recognized that further major developments, particularly computational prediction of total virus fitness in new hosts, would still be required for realizing the utility of computational tools in policymaking.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for future utility of computational tools.

claim: There is a need for better understanding of the evolutionary mechanisms and pathways that allow adaptive mutations controlling host range to appear and rise in frequency.
source: In addition to the genotype–phenotype relationship itself, there is a need for better understanding of the evolutionary mechanisms and pathways that allow adaptive mutations controlling host range to appear and rise in frequency.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Evolutionary mechanisms act in reservoir hosts, in intermediate hosts (if any), and in humans or other potential hosts.
source: These mechanisms act in reservoir hosts, in intermediate hosts (if any), and in humans or other potential hosts; they also act at multiple scales, as viruses compete for replication within hosts and transmission between hosts (Park et al., 2013, Russell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2013 and Russell et al., 2012.

claim: Viruses compete for replication within hosts and transmission between hosts at multiple scales.
source: These mechanisms act in reservoir hosts, in intermediate hosts (if any), and in humans or other potential hosts; they also act at multiple scales, as viruses compete for replication within hosts and transmission between hosts (Park et al., 2013, Russell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2013 and Russell et al., 2012.

claim: Developing better phylodynamic model frameworks for modeling virus host transfer and adaptation will require collaboration between theoreticians and experimentalists.
source: Developing better phylodynamic model frameworks (Grenfell et al., 2004) for modeling virus host transfer and adaptation will require collaboration between theoreticians and experimentalists.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement, with citation to Grenfell et al., 2004 for phylodynamic frameworks.

claim: There is tremendous variety in the structures of oligosaccharides displaying sialic acids and in the structure of the sialic acids in different avian hosts.
source: However, in addition to the α2,3 and α2,6 linkages, there is a tremendous variety in the structures of oligosaccharides displaying the sialic acids and in the structure of the sialic acids in different avian hosts (Gambaryan et al., 2012, Jourdain et al., 2011).

claim: The binding specificity for each receptor variant form may affect the potential for different viruses to cross the species barrier.
source: The binding specificity for each receptor variant form may affect the potential for different viruses to cross the species barrier or make the difference between causing severe or only mild disease.

claim: The acquisition of samples entering existing surveillance networks is largely ad hoc.
source: However, the acquisition of samples entering existing surveillance networks is largely ad hoc, exhibits substantial variation by host and geographical region, and only a small proportion of the data end up in the public domain (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about current surveillance practices, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The sudden proliferation of a previously rare virus subtype could indicate the emergence of new viral variants in non-human hosts that should be prioritized for further study.
